summary:
Barrilete Cósmico is a simulator that helps astronauts monitor their own health on deep-space missions, where contact with Earth can be delayed by many minutes. A wristband and a suit provide simulated data on vital signs, radiation, sleep and stress to a system that runs entirely on board.

It does not only report what has already affected the astronaut. It also anticipates risks to physical and mental health, so they can be handled before they become emergencies. The system tells the astronaut how to proceed, from taking shelter during a solar storm to adjusting work and rest, without depending on anyone outside the spacecraft.

Data is stored on board and sent to Earth after the communication delay, so Mission Control stays informed but is not needed for the first response.

All values are simulated. Safety limits come from NASA-STD-3001 and NOAA data, and solar events from NASA DONKI.
details:
What it does

Barrilete Cósmico is a web prototype that simulates health monitoring for astronauts on missions where communication with Earth takes about 20 minutes each way. A wristband with LEDs and a suit with lights on the chest show each astronaut’s status in green, yellow or red. The app lets you pick one of four astronauts, each with their own baseline data, and every module switches to that person.

How it works

The system reads pulse, blood oxygen, temperature, blood pressure, glucose, sleep, mood, exercise and radiation. Local rules on board compare each value with that person’s own baseline and set the alert level, with no cloud needed. Data is stored in a SQLite database inside the browser and sent to Earth with the simulated delay. If the link drops, data piles up and is resent later. Four modules work together:

Radiation: shows the dose rate, the time left before the career limit (600 mSv) or a single-event limit (250 mSv), and a countdown to reach the shelter when a solar storm is announced.

Habitat: simulates cabin CO2 and turns on ventilation automatically, with simulated MQTT-style messages.

Crew friction: calculates a tension index between crewmates, reshuffles shifts and suggests a shared activity. Earth receives only an anonymous summary.

Task planner: gives risky tasks to the crewmate with the lowest dose and the least tension.

Benefits

The ship responds on the spot instead of waiting 40 minutes for a round trip. Chest lights give warnings without blocking the astronaut’s view. Comparing against a personal baseline avoids false alarms for people whose normal values differ from the average. Crew privacy is protected, and no data is lost when the link fails.

Expected impact

This is a simulated prototype and has not been measured in real use, so these are expected effects. We expect to shorten the time between detecting a risk and acting on it, from tens of minutes to seconds, and to reduce radiation overexposure by reassigning tasks. We also expect to give the commander clear information to decide with. The same logic could serve isolated places on Earth with limited communication.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file that runs in any browser, with no server.

Storage: SQLite compiled to WebAssembly (sql.js).

Animation and design: GSAP with ScrollTrigger, and the Bricolage Grotesque typeface.

Build and testing: a Python script assembles the final file, and Playwright runs automated tests.

Real reference data: the NASA DONKI API for solar events, NASA-STD-3001 for dose limits, NOAA SWPC for storm frequency, and measurements from the Curiosity RAD instrument.

AI assistance: the code was developed with help from Claude (Anthropic), which belongs in the AI-use declaration.

Hardware: no physical hardware was built. The wristband, the suit, MQTT and SCADA are simulated on screen.

How it is creative

It brings together what is usually handled separately: vital signs, radiation, cabin air and crew relations. Crew friction is private by design: the ship acts and Earth never sees names. The lights sit on the chest so they never block the visor. The planner uses the same data as everything else, so a change in radiation, sleep or relationships rewrites the whole schedule. There is also a touch of humor: if an astronaut doesn’t reach the shelter in time, crosses appear over the eyes on the visor.

Factors considered

Communication delay and link loss, the real NASA dose limits, individual differences between astronauts, privacy, mental health alongside physical health, and keeping the astronaut’s view clear. We also considered accessibility (each alert level blinks at a different pace, not just a different color, and the reduced-motion setting is respected), interface simplicity, and honesty about the simulation: the values are invented and the on-board “AI” is a set of rules.

Our hardware system was designed with future upgrades in mind, aimed at improving spacecraft maintenance and astronaut comfort. Plans include expanding the autonomous agent system, implementing data persistence, and creating a mission control interface.
